title: The Success and Failure of Retrieval Practice in England
author: Unstoppable Learning
summary: This piece argues that England's widespread adoption of the term 'retrieval practice,' now part of every teacher's vernacular, has become a hollow success: the vocabulary spread faster than genuine understanding of the underlying mechanism, so that most teachers' grasp of the concept is barely deeper than a layperson's, without reference to forgetting curves or storage strength. The author identifies the specific failure mode driving this gap: teachers ask 'did today's lesson have retrieval practice in it?' when the correct question operates at the level of accumulated knowledge across an entire course, not any single lesson, asking whether everything previously taught is being adequately and optimally spaced for retrieval. The piece makes a specific, counterintuitive numerical claim: most maths lessons currently spend roughly 20% of time on retrieval and 80% on new content, and argues the ratio should be closer to inverted, 80% retrieval and 20% new teaching, once a course has been running for a few weeks. It profiles Lee Wheeler's 'Learning Engine,' a tool that tracks everything taught at the level of individual knowledge items and automatically schedules spaced retrieval, noting that some auto-generated lesson plans eventually require zero new content because so much prior knowledge needs consolidation. The piece closes by comparing Wheeler's results to Dr Dario Emanuele's, framing both as evidence that a much higher retrieval ratio than teachers currently believe feasible produces faster, more durable learning once the accumulation is properly tracked.
points: Argues that England's success in spreading the term 'retrieval practice' into every teacher's vocabulary has outpaced genuine understanding of the mechanism, leaving most teachers' grasp barely above a layperson's without reference to forgetting curves or storage strength.

Identifies the specific failure mode precisely: teachers ask whether today's lesson contained retrieval practice, when the correct question operates at the level of all previously taught knowledge across a course, not any single day's lesson.

Makes a specific, counterintuitive numerical claim that most maths lessons currently allocate roughly 20% of time to retrieval and 80% to new content, arguing the better ratio inverts this to roughly 80% retrieval and 20% new teaching.

Profiles Lee Wheeler's 'Learning Engine,' a tool that tracks taught content at the level of individual knowledge items and auto-schedules spaced retrieval, noting some generated lessons eventually require zero new content due to accumulated retrieval demand.

Frames the payoff as counterintuitive but empirically supported: slower learning in the first weeks and months under a retrieval-heavy structure, followed by dramatically accelerated learning once the compounding spacing effect takes hold.
quotes: So, it is a great success that retrieval practice is a term you can expect any teacher in England to have squarely in their vernacular. Yet, many people have spoken recently about retrieval practice as a 'lethal mutation.'

Without reference to forgetting curves, the New Theory of Disuse, memory retrieval and storage strength, or the history of the testing and retrieval effect, teachers' understanding of retrieval practice is not much greater than that of a layperson's.

The question should never be 'did today's lesson have retrieval practice in it?' The right question is 'does all of the mathematical knowledge my students have learnt up to now have adequate retrieval practice, optimally spaced, so that the storage strength of their memories is maximised?'
Most maths lessons today spend 20% of their time on retrieval, and 80% teaching something new. The better split is more like 20% of their time teaching something new, and 80% on retrieval.

Lee has even said that some lessons require so much retrieval that there is zero new learning for that lesson. And yet, much like Dr Dario Emanuele, Lee is finding that his students are learning more, and progressing faster, than ever before.
